utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Milosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The cross-examination by Mr. Hannis will now continue. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you gave at the beginning of your evidence continues to apply to that evidence today. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Milosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to go back to one thing I spoke about with you yesterday just to complete the matter, and the first time this came up was when Mr. Fila was asking you about the delivery of humanitarian aid in Kosovo and whether or not there had been any discrimination in its distribution, and you told us that you didn't see any discrimination. And this was at page 14281, line 1. The very next question he asked you was: "Were you a member of the SPS?" And your answer was: "No, I was not a member of any party." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And I wasn't, not when I was appointed to the cabinet of Serbia. I said yesterday that I had been a member of the League of Communists until 1989 when I was expelled after what happened at the eighth session. As for your question, whether I was a member of any party afterwards, I did say that I joined the Yugoslav Left and I was a member of that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to clarify. I did ask you about that, and you told me that you were not a member of any party when you were chosen to become a government minister, and I understand that you became a minister on the 21st of March, 1994. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I became a minister after the national assembly election on the 21st of March, and as I said, I remained in that position until 1998, but at that point in time I was not a member of any party. I was elected as a non-party candidate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you told us that you didn't become a member of the Yugoslav Left until 1995 after you had already become a minister; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you were not a member of JUL before you became a minister were you -- were you an affiliate or some kind of candidate on a JUL ticket?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at the time. I was a candidate for the Yugoslav Associated Left. The, I think, 1993 election there was a mixed bag, that group of intellectuals and professors. We were on their list but we didn't do anything. We didn't get past the election threshold and we didn't make it into the national assembly, but that wasn't the JUL.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that the predecessor for the JUL?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was called the Yugoslav Associated Left. It wasn't a party. If you really want to know, there were people involved who later became members of the JUL, but there were many people involved in that group who never became members of the JUL.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you Exhibit P2910, and I have a hard copy for the witness, Your Honour. If the usher could help me. Mr. Milosavljevic I'm going to show you a document this is from the Official Gazette of Serbia for I think it's the 8th of December, 1993. Do you see that date highlighted at the top of the page? I've highlighted it in pink on your copy.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if you would go to the second page in your document. In e-court it is page 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I only have the original, Your Honour. I don't have an English translation, but just a couple things I'll have the witness read for us and I think that will suffice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On that next page, sir, at the bottom left, item number 2114. I've highlighted the title. Could you -- could you go back to the second page and read what I've highlighted on that second page? Not the one you have in front of you right now, sir. Yes. Not that. Can you go back one page for me, please. Yes. And that highlighted portion, item number 2114. Could you read the title of that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Decision to appoint a collective electoral list for the appointment of national delegates to the national assembly of the Republic of Serbia and the electoral unit 8 Smederevo list Socialist Party of Serbia list headed by Slobodan Milosevic. Is that sufficient for your purposes, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And then if you can go to the next page and this is page 35 in e-court on the bottom right item number 9 I've highlighted. Could you read those two highlighted sections for us, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Number 9, the associated left (League of Communists movement for Yugoslavia. Association of Serbia's Workers, Yugoslavia's national fronts, the youth league movement for Yugoslavia list, headed by Professor Mira Markovic." There follows a list of candidates. The first candidate is Dragan Kostic; followed by doctor of medicine Prvoslav Markovic; followed by Andreja Milosavljevic, a lawyer; a factory manager and so on and so forth. Am I supposed to go on reading those names out for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's fine you can stop there thank you. So is your testimony you were not a member any party at this time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I wasn't a member of any party. This is an association, as you see, and it combines all sorts of things, the League of Communists, the Movement for Yugoslavia, Serbia's Workers Association, the National Front, the Youth Association, and the Movement for Yugoslavia. So this is a broad front so to speak containing candidates from all sorts of different bodies and groups. Our intention being to make it into parliament as a parliamentary group such as the Associated Left. That was the intention behind this grouping. There are many persons here on this list who were not members of any party at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And this -- this group was headed by Mira Markovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the time I was in contact with the president of the Movement for Yugoslavia. As for Mira Markovic, I only attended a single rally in a village somewhere. Three days before the election I myself came forward. It wasn't Mira Markovic who did. I think it was the president of the Movement for Yugoslavia, a professor whose name I can't remember right now. Another person who spoke at that rally on behalf of the Workers Party. Again I can't remember the name. Another person on behalf of the Workers Association. I was a non-party candidate and my task at this final pre-election meeting was to speak about agriculture and what developments we envisaged for agriculture as well as the objectives that we would be advocating once we became members of the National Assembly. Professor Mira Markovic was not present at this gathering. And the same goes for other gatherings. This was our pre-electoral complain and most frequently I've --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You've answered the question. The document itself though says that she heads the list; correct? Isn't that what that document says?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what the document says. However, we acted based on agreements that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me move on to something else then. Yesterday you were talking about the -- your task when you were appointed to coordinate the state organs in Kosovo, and you mentioned that one of the things you did, this is at page 14259, you said: "I was especially tasked with establishing the reasons for the setting up of municipal councils in the municipalities where elections had not been held or had been held but were irregular, and then the government of the Republic of Serbia established municipal councils whose task was to replace the work of the Municipal Assembly and its Executive Committee." Why was it necessary to replace municipal assemblies and Executive Committees by these other bodies called municipal councils?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that I spoke about this. I do have to express one reservation. I didn't say municipal wards, I said municipal councils, but that is essentially the same. There was a legal basis for setting up these municipal councils. This was the law on territorial organisation of the Republic of Serbia and the law on self-government, Article 45 and Article 64(A) of this law specifically, and I can't quote these texts from the Official Gazette just off the bat, but the regulations are there, envisage that in such municipalities where no elections can be held which means the voters don't participate cannot continue to function in the absence of proper organs. They don't have a Municipal Assembly which was the supreme body of government within any municipality and they don't have executive boards as the supreme bodies of the executive in any municipality. There were the -- eight such municipalities, as I said, and the government of the Republic of Serbia, based on their legal powers, passed appropriate decisions to establish municipal councils for those municipalities. Those decisions stated, in clear and precise terms, that the municipal councils were now there to stand in for the municipal assembly and for the executive, a board of the municipal assembly as its executive body. At the same time, the government made proposals for individual appointments to these municipal councils. These normally numbered between 7 and 13 members. Also --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have we not got the answer a little while ago, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, we had -- we also got an answer to the next two questions I was going to ask so I just let him go on a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So one of the differences between municipal assemblies and these municipal councils is that municipal assemblies members were elected by the citizens in the municipality; correct? And the Municipal Council members were appointed from outside by the government; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. However, I must say this by way of clarification. There were municipal councils that were introduced in other parts of Serbia in a total of 11 other municipalities. But there is a difference, the Municipal Council is elected by secret vote by all the citizens of a certain municipality whereas the councils are appointed by the government. It is envisaged that these municipal councils would be re-elected after, for example, a year if a new election is scheduled. Or if no election is held, the same measures continue to apply by appointing municipal councils and their individual members.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you said -- I see Mr. Zecevic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I believe the witness said 11 municipalities in other parts of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I thought that's what I heard too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your earlier answer, sir, I think you said there were -- there were eight municipalities where this happened. You mean eight municipalities in Kosovo where municipal councils were set up?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall which eight municipalities by name?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll do my best. Stimlje, Decani, Djakovica, I will remember eventually, it's just that it's too many things at once. Glogovac, Kacanik, Orahovac, elections were held there at a later stage, and regular bodies were set up as a result. At one point in time the situation occurred in Srbica as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's -- that's pretty good. I -- I don't need you to carry on unless you think of it later. And were these municipal councils all set up during your time as coordinator or did they happen before you went down there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipal councils that I'm talking about were set up during my time as a member of Serbia's cabinet. For your information, they were around even before that time in some of the municipalities. As for Kosovo, the situation was quite peculiar since in those municipalities the elections had failed, with the exception of Djakovica municipality where measures were applied, although the Socialist Party was in power at the time. Because of the fact that it wasn't operational I went there, I took in the situation and I proposed that special measures be taken although there were members of the Socialist Party in power. President of the municipality, a young man, was a socialist himself and most of the local set-up were socialists. They just didn't do their job well. There were a number other problems occurring so this was all under Article 45, the law on territorial organisation of the Republic of Serbia and self-government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving to another topic. You told us that in March of 1998 you were chosen to be part of the -- the government delegation that was tasked with trying to conduct negotiations with the Albanian leaders and you referred to, I think, Exhibit 1D78, which was a document saying that this had taken place on the 10th of March, 1998. This was a delegation headed by Professor Markovic. Who -- who picked you to be part of that delegation?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was picked by the government of Serbia. If you look at the statement you will see that. I'm talking about the exhibit that you just mentioned. The delegation was headed by Professor Ratko Markovic and it also comprise the two other ministers in addition to myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you say the government though, was there a particular individual who picked you? Who told you you were going to be on that delegation or were you asked ahead of time if you were willing to serve? How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened I had been consulted by the prime minister in a way, and then he made a proposal to the cabinet. It was said that I should be a member of that delegation because I had been in charge of the matters to do with self-government over there and I was quite privy to what was going on in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did the prime minister give you any briefing about what you and this group were supposed to do as far as your specific task?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We certainly knew ourselves that this was about organising dialogue and about looking for a solution for Kosovo and Metohija to get on as usual, but we didn't have a chance to prepare for long. I just went through some documents myself to freshen up a little. I read the UN charter. I read the Paris charter of the OSCE framework convention on dealing with general issues by the Council of Europe, all the international and world standards that applied and were well-known. I read the government programme and the constitution of the Republic of Serbia. I just tried to bear all of this in mind, and then one afternoon and I had been given only a very brief time to prepare, I met with Professor Ratko Markovic. A plan was drawn up for him to be in charge. I can say that what I was doing down there was within the usual set-up that prevailed. I spoke about local self-government, how it worked, and then of course people raised issues because you see, it is the majority that decides over there and since in most of the municipalities --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You've gone beyond my question. My next question has to do with the timing of the setting up of this delegation. The 10th of March was, I think, just about five days after a MUP operation in the Decani area that led to the death of Adem Jashari and several members of his family and relatives, including women and children. Were you -- were you aware of that incident? There was a lot of publicity about that in the area, I understand.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I read about this in the press. There was a lot written about this. It was published on TV. Therefore, it wasn't something that went unnoticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in answer to Mr. Fila's question yesterday, you said the reason for the cabinet deciding to send your group there was because "we wanted to have a dialogue. And the cabinet was in favour of that." And I suggest to you the reason that you wanted to have a dialogue at that time was because the Jashari incident had generated a lot of international attention from the media and the diplomatic corps, and that was why this body was created at that time. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't. We had been persistently trying to get in touch with the leaders of the Albanian parties. However, it just wouldn't happen. But that was not the reason for this negotiating team to be established, and it certainly wasn't the only reason. The chief reason was our good intentions to hold talks in a bid to find solutions for the problems that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said it certainly wasn't the only reason. Are you allowing for the possibility that it was one of the reasons?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that even earlier on we tried to deal with this in that way. I can say that efforts were made to achieve just that. When I was in the area, I toured the municipalities in a bid to come to grips with this problem. I tried to establish some form of contact. I tried to organise talks. I tried to get everybody to talk their way to a solution and to keep everything in keeping -- in line with the regulations that prevailed at the time and that remain to prevail. It was a problem that one had to deal with because the functioning of the local government wasn't smooth. In those municipalities the Albanians simply refused to take part in the elections and we could not hold elections without the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You've answered my previous question. You told us that you stopped being a member of this negotiating team when the new cabinet was formed, and I think you told us that was late March 1998. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. When the new cabinet was appointed I was no longer a member of this delegation. This negotiating team was established sometime just after this at the very outset. I can't be certain now. I think I was there once or twice in April but this is of no consequence since nothing was achieved. At least what we had expected was not achieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So if this group was formed on the 10th of March and you were off by late March, you were really part of this group for three weeks or less?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took part in the work of the team, and these were government representatives. The negotiators could only be from the government of Serbia. That is why I was relieved of this duty and not just I, but also Ratomir Vico who also was not a minister later on. Professor Ratko Markovic remained because he was deputy prime minister at the time of the elections and when there were new elections he was elected again, and that is why he remained a member of the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During those three weeks that we -- that you were on the team, you told us that you recall you tried to have meetings with the Albanians about seven or eight times. Do you personally know whether or not notices about those meetings were delivered and received by the Kosovo Albanians you wanted to meet with? Do you have any personal knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I do have personal knowledge, because the head of our delegation, Mr. Ratko Markovic, checked this out. And I know on one occasion, we were at a cabinet meeting, he telephoned the chief of the Kosovo district and he asked whether the notice had been delivered, that negotiations would be conducted on such-and-such a date. The answer was yes. And on one occasion, when we were in Pristina, Professor Ratko Markovic said again that this invitation was compulsory and that it had to be handed to the leaders of the Albanian parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But that again is -- is not your personal knowledge. This is something that was told to you by somebody else; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I could not give better information except if I personally had handed in the invitation. I heard him say to the head of the Kosovo district that he should do this. I didn't check. I didn't get a feedback whether the invitation was signed or not. That is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You described your -- your job as being to coordinate the work of all state organs, state bodies, and to work in line with the constitution and all the positive laws and any decrees. Was -- did you have any further job description than what I've just read out or was that basically your job?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I need to clarify what my job was. I coordinated the work of civilian bodies. I had no jurisdiction when it comes to the military and the Ministry of the Interior. And of course the political relationships that were in evidence over there, that didn't interest me. I acted exclusively as a person responsible for the civilian sector, and I tried yesterday to explain what I actually did over there, and that is what I did right up until the moment when I left. Not of my own free well but -- but, rather, because I fell ill, as you told you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that. And one of the -- one of the things that's set forth in the decision appointing you to this position of coordinator is that you were to be report directly to the prime minister at least once a week, and I think you told us that you did do that. You reported to him at least once a week; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. At least once a week. I would go to see him to brief him, and sometimes during the week we would have telephone contacts and I would inform him of things that I considered to be important to speed things up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition to the personal contacts and telephone calls did you send him any written reports about your work?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On several occasions I did send written reports, but let me be more specific. On three occasions. One was a lengthier one as far as written reports are concerned. As for orally, we had these personal contacts. I would go to Belgrade as a rule once a week. Now, whether it was Saturday or Sunday or a Monday I can't remember now. I believe that not to be very important. But I did inform him, that is quite true. And it would usually be in the morning. I would take advantage of the occasion to talk to certain ministers when I needed their assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we're off -- we're off the subject again because what Mr. Hannis wants to know is about the written reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And my next question is about that. Do you know where those reports would be now, where they're archived, or do you have a copy of the three reports you sent?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that the written reports are in the government of the Republic of Serbia. I did have my own copies, but when I came from Kosovo, because I suddenly left Kosovo, my driver carried those reports to the government of the Republic of Serbia where I had an office, but because of the bombing a bomb fell there and destroyed not just those reports but other documents that I had. One written report, if I need to point this out as well, during the trial of Mr. Milosevic I handed to him. Now, where that ended up I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know which one of your three reports you gave to Mr. Milosevic? Was that the lengthy one you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the first report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is the first report the lengthy one?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first report was on two typed pages listing exactly all the activities I engaged in. I think it was at the end of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about something else. In Exhibit 2D356 -- this was a document from the Ministry of Finance, and you told us that this was a document you received similar to ones you received from most of the ministries advising you of who was going to be your contact person in connection with your work. You say most of the ministries. Can you tell us which other ministries besides finance that you got letters like this from? Or if it's easier can you tell us which ministries you did not get letters from, whichever list is shorter.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reports of this kind, similar reports, I received from the ministry of agriculture, the ministry of civil engineering, the ministry for local self-government, the Ministry of Health, and a similar one from the commodity reserves because supplies were needed from that source. So I think those are all the ministries I received such reports from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that in your work as the coordinator this meant coordinating the work of the ministries of the Republic of Serbia. The presidents of the municipalities and also it goes without saying you worked with the special organs such as the cadaster office and revenue office. What's the cadaster office? Can you explain briefly what that is and what it does?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cadaster service is a service which keeps a register of the entire property in a particular area within the framework of its rights and duties. I believe in Kosovo all the municipalities had such a cadaster service. These are measurements of property. Ownership is registered. What property is socially owned, what is state owned, what is privately owned, what is cooperative property. So that is the service that was established virtually in all the municipalities. I would even go so far as to say that all the municipalities had to. I didn't check each and every one, but I do know that all the municipalities were obliged by the law, even the smallest once, to have such a cadaster service which functioned very well. The employees of that service were surveyors, engineers, maybe technicians who were trained in the field, in that area. All the property, land, buildings, factories, water supply systems, electricity piles, and everything else that existed in Kosovo was registered in that service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That ownership information contained in the cadaster records, does it also indicate the ethnicity of the owners or is that something that would only be inferred from the name?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was specifically indicated Janko Jankovic, owner of land plot such-and-such. Salih Berisha, owner of a house, land plot such-and-such. In those records, cadaster records, because I had to go and take a copy for myself. I never saw that it said what my ethnicity was. Janko Jankovic, a Montenegrin -- I don't know what. But for your information let me also add that the cadaster service was under the supervision of the republic. Sometimes it was attached to districts. This varied in the course of history.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, the reason I ask is after special measures were imposed in Kosovo after 1989, weren't there some laws passed at certain restrictions on -- on the sale of property within Kosovo in terms about whether a Serb could sell property or to whom they could sell their property? Were you aware of any such prohibitions or limitations on the conveyance of private property?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a legal provision or any decree to that effect did not exist with regard to Kosovo and Metohija. There was a decree at the level of the Republic of Serbia as a whole. I think it was a decree. I'm not quite sure. I think it was not a law, which simply required that records be kept at the level of the of Finance Ministry in Serbia, in the government, in the ministry of finance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned in page 14270 some of the ministers and deputy ministers who -- who came to Kosovo during your time as coordinator, and you mentioned those who were permanently stationed and were in my headquarters or, rather, in my team." You referred to three men who had been assigned to you. I just want to be sure these are the same three persons. You mentioned the Assistant Minister for Labour and Social Matters, Mr. Kujundzic; the Assistant Minister for Agriculture, Slobodan Ilic; and someone from health. Were those the three persons that were assigned permanently to you in your job as coordinator? Or were you talking about someone else?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These three persons were directly under my control and they helped me in the technical respect and every other. Only with respect to the health ministry they changed. It wasn't always the same person, but Kujundzic and Ilic were always with me. Maybe on a day they may go to Belgrade. Kujundzic was permanently there but Slobodan Ilic left on and off, but there was a lot of livestock in Kosovo that needed to be taken care of then the danger existed of various infectious disease carried by livestock and so on. I don't want to waste more of your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila asked you about the kinds of problems you were dealing with. You mentioned that they were different and varied from municipality to municipality. You mentioned that sometimes it was health services and then you said there were problems in education. The problem with education was Kosovo-wide, wasn't it? Not just one municipality but that was a problem throughout the province of Kosovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is partly true. Education was functioning, but it wasn't regulated in the best possible way because Albanians did not attend the schools that the state had normally through its regulations established there, but instead they had a parallel educational system with their own curricula and that was the problem. And when speaking yesterday, I had in mind rather the preparations for the month of September, that is the new academic year, when after the talks of 3 plus 3 it was agreed that elementary and secondary schools should start work on the 1st of September, whereas the university should gradually start working in view of the repairs that had to be carried out with resources from the international community, but all this was agreed. And I can tell you that on the 1st of September in more than 90 per cent of the schools and kindergartens tuition started on the 1st of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Throughout Kosovo, the entire province?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean that schools were working throughout Kosovo. Yes, yes. The necessary conditions were ensured because until then secondary school pupils in certain municipalities went to separate premises. They wouldn't go to the schools that were in existence there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm a little confused because yesterday you were telling us about some of the problems in Kosovo when you went there in the summer of 1998, and one of the problems you talked about was several of the main roads that were -- were blocked and controlled by the KLA. If that's the case, how -- how were you able to open 90 per cent of the of schools in September?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the general view the situation in September was calming down, and it appeared that the problems would be settled in a satisfactory manner. It is normal that intensified efforts were made in that direction in the hope that things would move in a positive direction, and they did in many municipalities. I didn't do just this. Electricity did not exist in certain villages and municipalities. We regulated that. Telephone lines were also down in many municipalities. Then bus transport, et cetera, et cetera. So these vital daily problems were addressed, and during the summer after I left in July the schools were about to go on summer holiday and measures were taken for them to start working with the beginning of the academic year. There are documents to corroborate this and other sources. There was not my special area of responsibility. It was when problems arose in that area that I had some insight there. On behalf of the Ministry of Education, as a member of the negotiating team was the deputy or assistant minister, Mr. Milivoje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are we talking here about schools mainly for Albanian children or are we talking about something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are talking about all the schools, both for Albanian children and for Serb and other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before July were Serb children and those from other non-Albanian ethnic groups attending school regularly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Until the end of the school year and the preparations for the next year. It is possible that in view of terrorist actions which started at the end of March, it is possible that in some environments there was a risk, but mostly in all the other places the school year was completed normally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, sir, we've heard a lot of evidence in this case about the so-called education agreement which I think was signed in September 1996, but do you have any knowledge about whether that was ever implemented? I was of the understanding that that actually never got implemented. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with that agreement. I'm familiar with the agreement 3 plus 3, which with the involvement of the international community and work on it was throughout the summer and which was supposed to come into force in September, I'm not familiar with the details, but it envisaged the repairs of certain buildings in Pristina to accommodate student of both ethnicities and a process was initiated then which was about to be implemented. After I left as the university starts working in October, I'm not familiar as to what happened with the implementation of that agreement later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your answer was translated as certain buildings in Pristina to accommodate students of both ethnicities. By both ethnicities did you just mean Serbs and Albanians?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I meant the languages in which the universities were operating, but in practical terms that is what it was. But I think one needs a look at the agreement. It was signed. There was Balja [phoen] and some other people. Ratomir Vico, I remember. Percevic, Andjelkovic, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You've answered my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is a different agreement from the 1996 one I take it Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Right. The -- well, the witness doesn't presumably know the relationship. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You talked also about problems in the work of the courts and you agreed with Mr. Fila that there were many unresolved cases and you talked about priorities to be given cases. Which cases were given priority, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personal and property cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know who decided what -- or which cases would be given priority? Whose job was that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Judges and the courts and the presiding judges. And there were reinforcements from Serbia with judges because there was a shortage of judges in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija so from other district courts from the rest of Serbia, let me put it to you that way, judges were delegated to go there for a period of several months and they worked there in Kosovo and Metohija. This is common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where was your office when you were working as the coordinator? Was it in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My office when I was working as a coordinator was in Pristina, in the provisional administrative building. I think my office previously had been occupied by the president of the Executive Council of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand from your testimony or I gather from your testimony that you also went out in the field and visited several of the municipalities; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Not several, most municipalities in Kosovo and Metohija. I visited Kosovska Kamenica, Novo Brdo, Gracanik, Lipjan, Pristina, Vucitrn, Kosovska Mitrovica, Srbica, Pec, Decani, Dzakovica, Glogovac many times, Stimlje, Orahovac, Suha Reka, and so on and so forth. A total of 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I know there are 29, but you didn't visit all 29, did you? You said you visited several?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I visited the ones that I mentioned and I'm certain of that. I can specify the ones that I didn't visit, that I possibly didn't visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, that's okay. But from your answer I take it then that not all of main roads were closed all of the time because you were able to visit most municipalities that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From time to time the roads were blocked in one direction, for example, and then I couldn't travel. However, as soon as the roads were cleared I would go immediately to check what the situation was. This is the case of Decani, of Djakovica, of Orahovac, and so on and so forth. Srbica, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Fila asked you about if you were aware of some of the activities of the KLA and the -- during the time period that you were there in 1998, and your answer at page 14273 was: "I did not deal with that particular subject, but since I was there I have eyes and ears so I heard things and I even saw things. They, the KLA, carried out attacks here and there in different places. They kidnapped and even killed people." So you told us that wasn't your job. Did you have any regular contacts or briefings from the Ministry of Interior or the VJ about KLA activities? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that you had received a letter, and this Exhibit 2D372, which is a letter from Mr. Andjelko Kolasinac, Kolasinac, in Orahovac describing the situation there and asking for help from the security forces. You told us that you informed the prime minister about that letter, and he told you that he'd received the letter and that all measures would be taken. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Of course I do. I recall other things too that happened after that letter. I remember everything and everything that Mr. Kolasinac said eventually came true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you some questions about that. After the prime minister told you this were you aware that the -- that the MUP and the VJ took certain actions and carried out operations in the area of Orahovac later that month of July 1998?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time nobody informed me about what would be done and what steps would be taken. Mr. Kolasinac alone informed me on the 17th or possibly the 18th of July that there had been an incursion by the terrorists, the Kosovo Liberation Army, that they made their way into Orahovac and took the health station there. Of course we all know what happened. There was a severe crisis. Those forces captured a hundred citizens. 61 of those, mostly elderly people and children, were released, but 39 of those were taken away and never returned. As far as I know, afterwards when I read reports and when I spoke to the parents of those kidnapped or abducted, those persons were never returned. I later read in the press that those persons were never sent back. And this was the subject of my conversations with foreign diplomats and humanitarian organisations such as International Red Cross, UNHCR, various committees for human rights and so on and so forth. I was informed by him, but other municipality presidents would also tell me things like these despite the fact that we would normally meet for other matters. I didn't really have time to go into these things, to delve deeper into these things but it really wasn't my job, nor was I authorised to deal with these matters. I do know a little more about Orahovac and I know that soon after we sent out an appeal the municipality itself sent out an appeal, Mr. Kolasinac, for the displaced persons following the operation that was carried out by the security forces to be sent back to Orahovac and the other four villages populated by Serbs and indeed this soon materialised. We took measures for Orahovac municipalities specifically the town of Orahovac and the surrounding villages to function properly and indeed this was the case. We made sure they had sufficient supplies, all those who were returning and all those who were at risk. I know that the supply centre in Orahovac functioned properly. Even Albanians got their supplies there. There was an Albanian person who was a part of the team actually distributing aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of the operations carried out by the MUP and the VJ in late July in Orahovac area? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about the MUP. I was informed a day or two later but I don't know about the VJ. No one ever told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who told you about the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kolasinac, the security forces in line with their rules of service. It was just Kolasinac. Orahovac is not really that far from Pristina, about 56 kilometres, not even that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you now a document that's Exhibit P1468 in evidence. And if we can look at page 1 first. This is a lengthy document, sir, and I don't have a hard copy for you. Well, actually I can -- I do have a hard copy I can give you.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see the cover page is titled "Meetings of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija." If you would go to the second page, and I think you've got two-sided copies there. Yeah. If you could look at that page. There the first page is a meeting of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, 22nd July 1998. And further down can you see the list of those attending? Mr. Minic, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Andjelkovic, General Pavkovic, Mr. Djordjevic from the MUP, General Lukic, David Gajic, and a Milan Djakobic [phoen]. Now, I know you know Mr. Minic, Mr. Sainovic, General Pavkovic. Did you know General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you mean Sreten Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 6, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know the other 3, number 5, 7 and 8 on that list?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djakovic I think he was a colonel. I'd see him every once in a while, but not that often. As for Gajic, assistant chief for state security, I did see him once or twice or two or three times. As for Djordjevic, number 6, Djordjevic I don't believe I know that person, but I know all of these other persons on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And regarding actions taken in Orahovac, you'll see under Mr. Gajic on that page a second item. It mentions measures are taken in Prizren against eight persons from the territory of the villages Ratkovac, Orahovac, and Krusa for participation in terrorist actions. Is that what it says? It's the second bullet point under his name.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You can't see it or you can't read it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That's not what I'm saying. I see it. It says in Prizren also measures are being taken against eight persons from Ratkovac village, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of -- I don't know. I've never seen this before. I'm not familiar with this. I said yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- That I wasn't familiar with this topic of Joint Command except for at a later stage when the Milosevic trial first began I did hear of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that I'm just trying now to point to you references in these minutes regarding actions taken in Orahovac in late July. If you could go down after the one you just looked at go down one, two, three, four more and in English it's translated as after the blockade was lifted of the village of Orahovac the propaganda activities of Siptars is intensifying. Do you recall that around the 22nd of July the blockade of Orahovac had been lifted?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to Mr. Kolasinac's report I'm not sure about the exact date, but the gist was the security forces succeeded in driving the KLA forces back from Orahovac. So certainly the siege was lifted and Orahovac was now back in the hands of the regular forces, in the hands of the state, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And if you could go on down to Mr. Minic. I think he's the third name after that entry you just read, and he has a comment about Orahovac. I think it's near the --

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's on the next page; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And it's the second item under his name he says in Orahovac we need to resolve the issue of water and electricity and revive the civil life. Aid from prison will be on the way tomorrow. That sounds like the kind of work you were doing. Did Mr. Minic or any of these gentlemen attending this Joint Command meeting talk to you about the issue of water and electricity for Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the issue of water and electricity and other supplies in Orahovac I was addressed by the local authorities. I did everything I could within my jurisdiction. They did have a electricity problem and a water problem as well as other things there was a problem with their health unit too. Everything had been pulled apart. But it soon went back to normal. Mr. Minic didn't speak to me about this problem at all on the occasion that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Nor -- nor anybody else attending this meeting correct? None of these guys told you about it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none of them. I had my own channels, channels through which I operated. Municipality presidents and other municipality bodies. I did speak to Krsta about those early activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those early measures that were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, can you read the next entry under Mr. Minic's name? I want to be sure this translation is correct. It doesn't read well in English.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We shall deal with the electricity and water problem in Orahovac and bring the village back to life. Probably they're seeking assistance from Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's the next entry after that. One the last one under Mr. Minic's name. Yes, that one.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The military factor --" I can't read the last word. "The military factor is --" I can't know for sure. I don't know if this is an official document. It's difficult to read. I'm having difficulty finding my way around this document, and I don't quite understand. I'm not familiar with this. I'm not sure why you expect me to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm just seeking your help in --

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't as a matter of principle oppose an attempt to go through this, but it's difficult. I'd love to help, but apparently I'm unable to simply because I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This Joint Command, as far as I know, this is not really a legal term, is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's something that the Judges will be considering later on, but the copy you have in front of you is a typewritten copy, I believe; is that correct? It's handwritten. Is that handwritten?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This? Handwritten as far as I can tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm looking -- I'm looking at my handwritten copy and can you -- can you read the last word? Can you spell it out? On the copy I have it appears to be o-s-v-e, and I don't know if the next letter is a t or a j, and then a u. Osveju or osvetu. Isn't that what it is? And in e-court this is page 3. I don't know if we can put it on e-court and perhaps the interpreters can perhaps have a look. And it's near the --

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't strike me as very logical. "The military factor is approaching revenge," or something like that, but it doesn't make sense in terms language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Wait until the translation is finished. Thank you. Now, Mr. Fila. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what is this witness supposed to be doing? Is he supposed to now read something that he's never seen before? I don't see the purpose of this exercise. First he's being made to read something and then he says he can't and then again he's being forced to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, Mr. Hannis made it clear that he was anxious to ensure that this had been properly translated, and he was asking him to read the Serbian so that the interpreter would translate it because it doesn't make sense as translated in the document before us. Now, there's nothing wrong with that in the context of our work, which raises this type of problem from time to time. So he's asking us to read the Serb and then let's hear what the English translation is. So we will allow him to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, and I --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what, the interpreters cannot read the Serbian. Is he supposed to read it back for them? That's one thing I can't understand and one thing I try to point out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, this is often how to deal with this sort of problem to get someone to read the document from the Serbian so that we can hear exactly what these -- how these words are translated in case there's been a mistake made at another stage. So please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before the break I have just a couple of more of these that I want to ask you about, sir, and the next one is on, I think, page 8 -- or the eighth page of that document for you. And if you can see the printed numbers at the top of the pages it's a page number K0228419. They're in sequence, and if that helps you find it. Yeah, I think -- I think you have it now.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay this is page 8 of the B/C/S in e-court and page 9 of the English and I want to direct you to -- first of all this is a meeting apparently from the 24th of July and the first person speaking is listed as Mr. Gajo, who from other evidence I would suggest to you is probably Mr. Gajic. And the next to the last item under his name says: "After Orahovac uncontrollable robbing of Albanian houses started." Were you aware of that? Was that reported to you by the municipality president?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Municipality president informed me that cases of looting had occurred and misappropriation of property, but he didn't specify who this had been done by. He said these were village gangs trying to grab hold of some goods, some property. It wasn't on a massive scale because the authorities tried to deal with it to reduce it to as little as possible. He did say that these things were occurring, but that's all he said. And he said that people were taking advantage of this kind of situation to do that sort of thing, but he also said that measures were being taken to put a stop to this. He also said quite naturally that they would press charges against certain persons through appropriate bodies, and as far as I know at a later stage this was eventually done. Sometimes a misdemeanour judge could be called upon to prosecute these people or perhaps other bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you then to go to General Lukic which is just right below that and the second entry under his name --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, 32, 13, I believe the witness says the misdemeanour court can act promptly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That makes sense. Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And under General Lukic's name, this is page 9 of the English and page 8 of the B/C/S on e-court, the second item says: "25 members of MUP were sent from Prizren to Orahovac to secure the peace and order." Did the municipality president tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't discuss that sort of detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And right below that it says: "15, 16 Siptar bodies were found buried." Did he tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that there had been victims. My comment would be that these reinforcements and reinforcements from the security forces were quite a normal occurrence. It's not that he told me about this. What I'm saying now is my own comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, when you say he told you there had been victims, can you be more specific? Victims of what? By whom, and any other details he told you about victims? Not victims of the looting.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Victims of those clashes. He spoke about victims. I didn't dwell on that. I know that people had been killed. Some persons had been killed and had been buried. That's about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you tell the prime minister about that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That goes without saying. Not in detail, in general terms. I told him about the situation and about what had happened, to the extent that I was aware. I always believed that there were appropriate bodies doing their job, and this certainly wasn't my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. You can set that document to one side. I'm finished with that for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know I'm a minute early, but this would be a good point it take a break for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Milosavljevic, we have to have a break at this stage for 20 minutes. Could you please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we shall resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosavljevic, you told us yesterday when Mr. Fila was asking you about contacts with foreign diplomats and representatives of the NGOs, et cetera, that the prime minister had instructed you to -- to talk to them, and you started actually meeting with some of them as early as mid-June of 1998. Can you tell us briefly what direction or what did the prime minister tell you to do or to say when talking with those individuals, the foreign diplomats and NGO representatives?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct that the prime minister called me and told me to see foreign diplomats, ambassadors, and representatives of non-governmental and humanitarian organisations and to talk to them. He also told me to pay attention to informing them about my own activities, that is to focus on humanitarian aid, to secure conditions for the free movement of humanitarian aid and diplomats, also the activities of the government in taking adequate measures for the return of displaced persons to their homes. Also what specifically we're doing to ensure supplies for the population, how we were doing this, in what way, activities to repair houses, the provision of construction materials of various kinds for this to be done, and to provide other information that I was familiar with. I also later used the consultations I had with Mr. Sainovic for these talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, was it Mr. Sainovic's job, was he the one with the primary responsibility to deal with talking with foreign diplomats about Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic came to Kosovo and Metohija at the beginning of July, and as the vice-president of the federal government he was in charge of foreign policy, and it was his main task to coordinate and to talk to foreign representatives, diplomats, et cetera, and he did so at the higher level, if I may put it like that, with Hill and other personages there in Kosovo and Metohija. And with respect to us, he had a guiding role. This applied not just to me, because the diplomatic representatives wanted to talk to not just me but to everyone else, heads of districts, municipality presidents and I don't know who else. And people were not sometimes properly trained. This was their first opportunity to have such talks, so that we availed ourselves of assistance and instructions when we needed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were aware of the -- the three persons from the SPS who had been sent down in June 1998, Mr. Minic, Mr. Matkovic, and Mr. Andjelkovic. Did they have a role in talking with the foreign diplomats and the NGO representatives or do you know?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there they did not have talks with diplomats. Maybe an individual one here or there. Zoran Andjelkovic was a minister in the government of the Republic of Serbia. He was in charge of sports. So maybe he may have taken part in certain political talks. Mr. Minic could have conducted those talks. Mr. Matkovic was more interested in economic matters, as I said yesterday. That was his job. In view of the situation, the very difficult economic situation, some enterprises were not working at all. Others needed aid, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosavljevic, that's not the question. The question is whether they spoke to foreign diplomats, and it sounds -- well, you've made it clear you don't know, so let's move on. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, in a question to you about these talks, Mr. Fila said there were three or four delegations a day, and I don't think you really answered that. How many -- how many of these people did you talk to during your time there between June and the end of September 1998? Do you have any idea? Was it 20 or 200? How many of these kinds of meetings and discussions did you have?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be precise, but on a daily basis, on some days there would be talks with three or four delegations. Now, there may be diplomats or humanitarian organisations or journalists, on some days, but on the whole I think that this figure for the three-month period, and I also kept notes, I'm sure that that number would not be less than 50, because usually we didn't work Saturdays and Sundays. So that would be a minimum number. With many of them I had talks several times. For example, with the Red Cross representatives, or the UNHCR representatives. Sometimes I had to talk to them twice a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that one of the things that you talked with them about were measures that were being taken to repair houses that had been damaged or destroyed. Can you tell us what was actually being done about that? What measures were being taken to repair houses?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the requests of the government of the Republic of Serbia, in all municipalities which were exposed to such damage there were commissions formed to evaluate the extent of the damage and see how much material was required, and these commissions did their work. The government of the Republic of Serbia via the directorate for the development of Kosovo ensured the necessary construction material at several different locations; bricks, cement, windows, glass, and other necessities. This was stored in Orahovac, Decani, Klina, and Djakovica. These are the locations, Klina, Decani, Orahovac that I toured on a regular basis and also construction blocks, and there was an enormous quantity of building material of this kind stored there. I know specifically that in the village of Lade [phoen] windows were being glassed up. Citizens would come to pick up the glass and to repair the windowpanes. Minor repairs were done, and some houses started to be built in Klina. In other locations this was not possible. It was difficult to build new houses except in Klina and maybe some other settlements.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you have any -- do you have any concrete evidence, no pun intended, do you have any evidence in terms of photographs or documents showing actual houses that were rebuilt or repaired as a part of this programme? Are there any records about that that we can look at?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably there are. I don't have them, but I do know that in Orahovac and in the village of Ade, I went there with representatives of the UNHCR and it was our common view that things were happening in these two locations. Mr. Arboledo from the UNHCR was with me, and it was said that more glass was needed. As for Orahovac, there are photographs. There are photographs, because I went there to see that this was being done and it was done. I know that there were difficulties in Decani in that respect because there was a lack of interest. Even though there was an open invitation, the building material was piled in the middle of the settlement. And in Klina these activities were quite satisfactory and some houses were repaired there, and there was a programme for the construction of new ones. Now, the question was how much should be given in the form of material --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've long since answered that question. If Mr. Hannis wants the additional information he can ask for it. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know -- can you give us an approximate number of houses that were rebuilt, if you know? Was it 10, 50, a hundred?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In one of your answers to a question from Mr. Fila about people being kidnapped by the KLA --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you finished with the question of the damaged houses?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I have one or two questions about that. You -- you said, Mr. Milosavljevic, that houses had been damaged and destroyed, and these are the houses we've been talking about in the last few questions. Who did these houses belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These houses belonged to both Albanians and Serbs. There were destroyed houses, damaged houses on both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do you know how the Albanian homes were damaged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Like all other houses, they were damaged during the operations, the terrorist and anti-terrorist operations. There may have been some other causes. I heard a report that there was some -- there were some acts of revenge by individuals in villages, because this mostly happened in villages. Houses were destroyed, damaged in the villages, outside the towns. In those days the towns were safe in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I do have another question or two about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosavljevic, did you ever meet a press officer for the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees names Mons Nimberg?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can remember because there was so many. It is quite possible, but I can't be explicit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. He is reported as having said regarding the programme to build houses or furnish building material: "There's absolutely no evidence of the programme they've announced. I don't see how the government would have the resources to do the amount of repair necessary." Were you aware that that statement was being made about your programme to repair houses? This was being said in August of 1998.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I be given a reference? Could I see this statement and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sure you can get that from Mr. Hannis, but the question's been answered in a way that makes it not necessary immediately, so we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's contained in Exhibit P2911 for Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me -- let me move on to something else. You mentioned that you had a number of meetings with -- with families and relatives of persons who had been kidnapped, and you said there were 2 or 300 such cases while you were there in Kosovo. Between June and September of 1998, I take it. What was your source of information for that number of 2 to 300?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The source are the municipal reports which I received mostly because relatives and family of the kidnapped wanted to talk to me, and talking at these various locations I made this estimate. I think that the number was close to 300 or just over 300. I'm not quite sure, or maybe 229. I can't remember exactly the figure, just as I couldn't remember the names of the municipalities a moment ago, though I could enumerate them now. And talking to those parents and relatives I learned about these things, but there were also official reports in the municipalities. They were their citizens. It was not only Serbs that were being kidnapped but also Albanians and other ethnic groups, the Roma and others. This started on the 12th of May already when a worker in Bilacevac was kidnapped. Then on the 22nd of June, 8 persons were kidnapped, and then in Orahovac 39, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said these were municipal reports. Did they come from the police or from the president? Where were you receiving these reports from?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't receive reports from the police but from the municipal bodies, and sometimes from the chief of district, collective reports, because of these talks that I had, and there were between 10 and 12 such interviews with family members of the kidnapped and arrested persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned the republican commission for refugees. Who was the head of that commission in 1998? If you know.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was headed by Buba Morina, the Commission for Refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is Buba a nickname?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's her first and last name. At least that's how I knew her. It's possible that she had another name, but I know her as Buba Morina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned the -- how the distribution of humanitarian aid was done, and you told us that at the level of the Republic of Serbia headquarters were set up for distributing supplies to people in Kosovo. So there was a headquarters set up in Belgrade? Is -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how you understood what I said yesterday. I said that the government of the Republic of Serbia with its resources which were set aside for that purpose by appropriate decisions, and there are documents to that effect, decided that aid in the form of food supplies, medicines, and building material be distributed in Kosovo among displaced persons, returnees, and those in need of aid. In addition to humanitarian aid that went through the Red Cross of Yugoslavia, Serbia, and the province, and all the humanitarian organisations from abroad which provided very significant aid, the government of the Republic of Serbia also formed a central headquarters for supplying the population. When talking about the central headquarters, its task was to procure all the foodstuffs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosavljevic, the question was whether the headquarters were in Belgrade. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The central headquarters had its leadership in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it was working in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. If Mr. Hannis wants that additional information, he will ask for it. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will. I'm trying to clear this up. So this is at page 14285, and you said: "In parallel with this republic headquarters a province centre was set up as well." So I'm trying to figure out at the republican headquarters, is it just people in an office or were there actual warehouses and goods and humanitarian aid kinds of things sitting in Belgrade that were eventually distributed in Kosovo, or is it only the administrative personnel that you're talking about at the headquarters in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The central headquarters in Belgrade had the task of distributing all necessary goods in Kosovo according to needs. It did so out of the commodity reserves which existed in Serbia and in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And for instance, oil from the diamond factory in Vrbas and from other manufacturers, and sugar from I don't know which enterprises, had to channel these supplies to Kosovo. When the central headquarters decided about this humanitarian aid was free. There was a deficiency of goods, of certain goods, that went to all the population. And then there was a commercial basis also, because there was a danger of individuals forming surpluses and reserves, and this could cause problems down there, and that is why there was strict inspection to control this and these headquarters at the various levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who the people were that were in charge of the headquarters? Are we talking about one person or is this a group of 10? And who -- who appointed them or put them in that job?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This headquarters consisted of about 10 people, and heading the headquarters was the Minister for Agriculture, Mr. Babovic. Members were Minister of Internal Trade, Mr. Viskovic, people from the commodity reserves, and from various ministries. The -- this headquarters was formed by the government of the Republic of Serbia. I took part in its work. I said there were one or two meetings in Belgrade. The rest were always held in Pristina and also in the various districts when necessary. I remember meeting in the district of Kosovska Mitrovica and Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you told us that the humanitarian aid was distributed free of charge; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 14287, you said in one of your answers that: "The state took matters into its own hands in order to avoid shady situations which sometimes occur in this sort of context. There were companies that were in charge of this and these companies were closely watched." Sir, would you agree with me that sometimes activities run by the state can be shady as well?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree that it is possible for this to happen when the state is in charge, because every effort was made to make sure that the rules are respected and the decisions taken. Humanitarian aid was free of charge for displaced people, people in need, and at a later stage this went through humanitarian centres that were formed in the most afflicted areas. I said there were 14 such areas during the time I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, sir, you're -- you're an education the fellow. You're a young fellow about my age, and you've been active in many -- many levels of the government.
