Are you telling me that human beings who work in -- in the state are not just as subject to the foibles of non-state employees when it comes to shady activity? I'm not saying it happened in your commission or in this case, I'm just saying as a general principle. You're not aware of any instances of graft or corruption in your government in the last 20 years?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not just the last 20 years, but anything is possible where human beings are concern. What else can I say? As for any specific situations occurring, my knowledge would suggest a negative answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just asking you about the general principle right now. Who decided who got aid? I mean, was there -- was there more than enough humanitarian aid to go around for everybody who needed it, or -- or was it necessary sometimes to make choices between recipients of aid?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly one needed to prioritise, but every effort was being made for aid to reach those most in need, or everybody in need. What the specific destinations would be for humanitarian aid was dictated by the situation on the ground. I'm convinced that the assistance provided by the various humanitarian organisations was outstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I want to ask you about your contacts with foreign diplomats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How are we doing with your cross in general, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've just been alerted by my case manager that I'm running up on the time that Mr. Fila used. I probably need half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Give us a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We don't intend to stop you proceeding, Mr. Hannis, but it's -- we have a fairly strong feeling that this has not been a terribly productive exercise. It lacks some focus, and we would be grateful if you could perhaps focus it a bit more directly for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosavljevic, Mr. Fila asked you yesterday at page 14289: "What about these foreign diplomats. When they come to speak to you did they ever underline any concerns they may have had about possible crimes in Kosovo?" And your, and your answer at line 21: "It is true that these problems, the problems of looting on all sides, were mentioned. And this was happening throughout Kosovo and Metohija, and this is one of the concerns that were being underlined." Now, you mentioned that they were talking about looting and punch-ups and threats and incidents. Weren't they concerned about more serious matters like displaced persons, women and children in the woods, and killings by the Serb security forces? Isn't that what they were talking to you about rather than looting?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Foreign diplomats particularly wanted to know about the return of displaced persons to their hearths and homes. They also required us to take appropriate measures to that effect, and this was exactly what we did. It wasn't just because of what the government said should be done but also at the local level. We invited people to go back to their homes. Generally speaking, I believe the results were quite good. Needless to say, they wanted to know about other things, too, but more in order to get some information, at least to the extent that I could satisfy that need. They were asking questions about that, yes. There were other sorts of questions being asked as well. Questions from the security sphere were not so frequent. They knew that that was not my sphere of activity. Needless to say, it was necessary to stop the operations, but that cut both ways. It wasn't enough for me to ask one of the sides to stop. The other side was supposed to stop, too, for this to be a meaningful exercise. Of course they shared this view. They expressed concern about the entire situation. There were all sorts of people from all sorts of different levels talking to me. I remember a specific request by Mr. Satak [phoen], who was the US Deputy Foreign Minister. For example, if you look at the issue of humanitarian organisations, their interest was about one thing alone, how the aid issue was working, how displaced persons were being helped, and those arrested, and of course everybody wanted to know how the whole thing was going and what the state was doing about all these issues. What I did was inform them about all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understand security was not your issue, but the foreign diplomats that talked to you, including Ambassador Petritsch and others, even though you were dealing with humanitarian aid and displaced persons, they expressed the concern to you about the disproportionate use of force by the Serb police and the army, didn't they? Weren't they talking to you about that and complaining about that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were complaints like that being made, what is normally termed disproportionate use. I didn't really understand that, so I provided some clarification as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember being visited by a special representative of the UN Secretary-General for Children in Armed Conflict between September 10th and 12th 1998? The name of the person was Olara; O-L-A-R-A; Otunnu, O-T-U-N-N-U. She said she met with you, among other persons. Do you recall her, or him?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. There was sometime in early September, I believe. I can't any details, but I do recall that this person who was in charge of -- in charge of children's rights came to see me about something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this is Exhibit 2905. I'm sorry, I only have it in English. I want to read a couple paragraphs from her report. In her report she indicated: "Today it is estimated that some 300.000 people have been displaced by the fighting in Kosovo. Over 60 per cent of whom are children around over 20 per cent are women. About 50.000 of the displaced persons are stranded in the open in the mountains, in the woods." Were you aware that that's what the UN special representative was reporting about the situation in September 1998?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not aware with these specific figures in particular. I do know that talks were held and the concern was voiced that this should be closely monitored. The figures concerning the number of displaced persons were quite high at one point, 300.000. I don't know. I don't think there were that many. The usual estimate was between 200.000 and 230.000. It really depended on your source, where the figures came from and who provided the specific figures. I can say that I had a pretty realistic view of each and every one of these various situation. When I toured the municipalities I would ask questions about these matters. We had our own method of dealing with this. We knew the number of inhabitants in each and every one of the villages. People on the ground could tell us how many persons had left, and that's how we got our figures. But we always --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You've answered my question. Let me stop you there because I'm running short on time. Let me move to Pristina now, and if we could have Exhibit P615 at page 31 on screen. Can you tell us where you stayed when you were in Pristina? I think yesterday you told us you were living in the army corps building. Do you know where that was in Pristina? If we put the map up in front of you can you point it out for us? Hopefully it will be on your screen in a moment.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand your question. Where I was working or where I was sleeping?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. I can answer your question. I'm not sure if there's a map, but the building that I was working in was the building belonging to the provincial authorities, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosavljevic, there should be a map on the screen in front of you, and you'll be able to mark it in a moment. If the usher could assist you with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I know it's been a while, sir, and I don't know if you can recall.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I can, but I'm having some difficulty getting my bearings. It's to the right here. As for the street --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As far as landmarks go, I know number 93 is the Grand Hotel. I don't know if that helps orient you in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Number 93 --

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this way. The provincial authorities were right here at 40, 40 something, 46. In that area. And then you take the street that goes past the Grand Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you draw -- can --

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps was down that street and to the right from the Grand Hotel. You said 93; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you draw a circle around the approximate location of your office, please? Using that pen.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can describe it for you, but this is Pristina, the city of Pristina, and -- 93. I can mark the location roughly for you, the general location. It was like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps. Roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you could put a 1 in the first circle where your office was, roughly, and a 2 in the circle where the corps was?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you do two more for me. Do you know where the MUP was located approximately?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was to the right, this way from the corps and it should be around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Put a 3 in that one, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And finally where Mr. Minic, Andjelkovic, and Matkovic were during their time down there. Was that a different location?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in the SPS building, and I think it was in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you put a 4 in that circle.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is only defined in very rough terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I'm looking at these locations in relation to the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we give that an IC number, Your Honour? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC 138, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that these complaints that the foreign diplomats were giving to you, that you passed that information on to the prime minister even though it involved to some extent subject matter that was not your job to do, and you told us that Mr. Marjanovic told you that you should pay attention to the work that you were in charge of. Did he do anything to follow up on information you passed on to him about these complaints from the internationals, that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask, and he never said -- or, rather, he did say that, objectively speaking, even had I been willing to do that I couldn't have managed because I had my other job and I was spending a lot of time elsewhere touring the area; and I would always drive back to Pristina in the evening. I had no security, although I was in actual fact entitled to a security detail. I felt safer while driving around without security. There was my driver and two other persons with me as a rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned seeing Mr. Sainovic during your time in Kosovo in 1998, and Mr. Fila asked you what you knew about Mr. Sainovic's task while he was there. At page 14305 your answer was: "He told me this himself, and I also learned it from the prime minister. He was in charge of foreign policy, of talks with foreign diplomatic representatives, and he was in charge of coordinating all that." Did you tell Mr. Sainovic about what the internationals were telling you during your talks with them?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would meet Sainovic from time to time, and I would inform him about my job. Also, I would tell him about everything in quite informal terms. I would tell him about other observations that had reached me. So I probably shared this with him too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You've said that you asked -- you asked him to help you concerning certain issues. This is at page 14306. What issues did you ask Mr. Sainovic to assist you with?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply, I had no experience in meeting diplomats. I asked him about subjects that might be raised, that were likely to be raised, and how to talk to them. Understandably, if I may say, I wasn't trained for that sort of thing. I had met with foreign officials two or three times before, and what he told me was to do my best to keep foreign diplomats up-to-date in as much detail as possible as to my activities and any results that I was achieving. He also said that I should closely study possible effects and consequences, and he told me to take a thorough approach to all of this, to all of the explanations I was providing and to all these talks and contacts in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us that you had not heard of a body called the Joint Command before. I guess, you read about it in the papers after the Milosevic trial began. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I'd never heard that term before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever ask Mr. Sainovic about the Joint Command after you heard of it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd never heard of it, as I said, so I never asked him. No, not even after. Having learned about the Joint Command did I ask him? No, I didn't. We didn't meet much throughout that period. If we'd met, perhaps I would have raised the issue; but we just didn't see that much of each other throughout that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When was the last time you spoke with him?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Mr. Sainovic. Well, I can't quite pinpoint the exact point in time, but I think the last time we actually spoke was before the trial of Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, but there's one thing I want to know. How many hours has the Prosecutor used up? I will have a chance of examining my next witness today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It depends on the length of your re-examination, but the plan is that you will have the whole of the final session, and that may be a bit longer than otherwise would be the case for your next witness. And if you sit quietly there, you may get longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You did not hear of the Joint Command, but were you aware that Mr. Sainovic was meeting frequently in Kosovo in that summer of 1998 with Mr. Minic, Mr. Andjelkovic, and Mr. Metkovic, among others? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that I was meeting them. That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Maybe that's a translation. It says you were meeting with Andjelkovic, Metkovic and Minic. You personally?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, me personally too. And we would talk, keep each other posted as it were, what was being done, how far we had got. Andjelkovic spoke a lot to people in the specific areas and he would provide me with information that was helpful in my work. Minic spent most of his time in the party --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, if you don't take control of this, then really we will have to bring it to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. My question was were you aware that Mr. Sainovic was meeting with those three individuals? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you aware that in addition to those three he was also meeting with General Pavkovic and General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Occasionally I was meeting them. Maybe on two or three occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's not my question though. Were you aware that Mr. Sainovic, in addition to meeting with those three, was meeting with General Pavkovic and General Lukic? He was meeting with the five of them at the same time. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did say that. I met them two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two questions were asked, and now what we got was half an answer. The last question asked by Mr. Hannis is different from the previous one. It actually contains two questions. Were I to repeat it, I might come across as trying to influence the witness. Could he just repeat? There is no problem other than that. One by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't have much problem with this but maybe the witness has, Mr. Hannis, so could you put the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: First question: Were you aware that Mr. Sainovic, in addition to meeting with Minic, Matkovic, and Andjelkovic, was also meeting with General Lukic and General Pavkovic? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I -- I will take advantage of your guidance, Your Honour, but I have no further questions. There is one thing I would like to share with Mr. Hannis. The last exhibit where the drawing was made, it doesn't quite work, but if it means something to Mr. Hannis I don't oppose him going through that exercise again where the drawing was made, where the map was marked a while again. Other than that as far as I'm concerned this story is now over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you wish, you can go through the exercise and clarify it by re-examining the witness, but it's matter for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the problem? The problem is this is a poor copy. It's difficult to see the numbers on it. And each of the buildings that Mr. Hannis asked the witness about was marked with a number. If you look what he's marked as number 1, you will see that the witness referred to that. If you look at what he's marked as number 93, 77, 70, and that's that. But that is not consistent with the locations marked by the witness, and I'm not sure how I should deal with this, but I would like to give the Chamber a fair warning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't really understand the map. As far as I can tell, it was incomplete, and also it's -- it's poorly visible because I'm sitting too far from the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, Mr. Hannis chose to do it his way but you have the witness's answers marked on the map. You can also in due course rely, I think, on the marks -- the original map with its numbers, and that may be plenty of food for you when you make your ultimate submissions, but if you want the map to be improved, you can only do that now by re-examining the witness, and if you don't want to do that it's a matter for you. But let's make --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have the map. This can't be done on the map on the screen. We need to have an original map for the witness to see properly. What is shown on the screen is not good. He's an elderly gentleman and he can't see it properly. I don't see how I can correct it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You look at it now on the screen and tell me if you don't think he can see it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see either. I'm an elderly man too. As I'm in a hurry for the next witness, I prefer to believe Mr. Hannis is right than to cause a lot of trouble with this problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what you know is the actual buildings that the witness was trying to locate, and you will have other witnesses to whom you may be able to put the point that would clarify where these buildings actually are, and if you take the two lots of evidence together you will have the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour, but the map that is being shown to the witness, there are markings of the buildings that he asked the witness about, and you can see the buildings clearly. Thank you. I apologise for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosavljevic, that brings your evidence to an end. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our next witness, Your Honour, is Veljko Odalovic. He's waiting to be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Odalovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading out loud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Mr. Odalovic. Tell us first of all what is your name, where you were born, and what is your occupation.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Veljko Odalovic. I was born in Kosovo and Metohija, Velo municipality, of Lipjan, on the 26th of August, 1956. By education I am a qualified lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Tell us about your professional career and what positions you held in the period since 1992.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: I started my career in Kosovo Polje working in various sports organisations. Later when Kosovo Polje municipality was formed I was president of the commission to prevent the displacement and encourage the return of the displaced. Later I became head of the legal department, assistant chief of the district, deputy head of the district, and from 1998 I was head of the Kosovo district.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you elected deputy -- were you elected as a deputy to the Assembly of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? It will be best if you look at the transcript and when you see the letters stop then give us your answer.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: At the parliamentary elections in the year 2000, I was elected deputy to the then Assembly of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the Chamber of Citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you head an assembly body as of 2004?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: In 2004, upon the initiative of a group of deputies supported by the parliament a board of inquiry was set up to establish the facts regarding the kidnapped, killed, and missing persons of Kosovo and Metohija. I headed that subcommittee for the inquiry.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What institutions, organisations, and services did you cooperate with in performing these duties?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that this was an issue that no one had dealt with up until then fully and that full agreement was reached among all the parties in the parliament of the then Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, we decided as board of inquiry to address as many domestic and international factors and individuals who could give us the facts about the kidnapped and missing, to have interviews with them, to collect as much information as possible, and to submit a report to parliament which would be the first such document that would have been made public regarding all the victims in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija regardless of any differences, all the persons who were killed in Kosovo and Metohija since 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My question was which -- the names of the institutions you cooperated with.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: As for the institutions we talked to we addressed the non-governmental sector, the fund for humanitarian right, the Helsinki Board for Human Rights, representatives of state bodies, representatives of the MUP, or the police, the army. We addressed the International Red Cross Committee, the UNMIK offices that were in Belgrade, the Red Cross of Serbia. We tried via UNMIK to get in touch with representatives of Albanians, that is the Association of Kidnapped and Missing Persons, to try to talk to them to collect as much reliable information as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What position do you hold now?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: Currently I am in head -- the head of a Commission of the Republic of Serbia for Missing Persons. This is a volunteer post. I am dealing with missing persons from the territory of the former Yugoslavia, which means in Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Serbia, or Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is the name of the commission?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: It is the Commission for Missing Persons for the government of the Republic of Serbia appointed by the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are you dealing in any other way with the destiny of the missing persons?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: As a result of the board of inquiry which has completed its work, the initiative was taken to continue the dialogue that was started between Belgrade and Pristina. This was started in Vienna in 2003. Covic Hekrup [phoen] but because of the March events in Kosovo and Metohija it was suspended. After that it was resumed and I am the head of the Belgrade delegation with three other representatives. Pristina had it's delegation headed by Mr. Bajazit Nushi who was also the head of the Department for Human Rights, and Mr. Francois Stamm the chairman of this working group as a representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you go to Kosovo and Metohija nowadays?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I go there regularly. Less than two months ago we had a meeting of the working group in Pristina and a similar such meeting will be held in Belgrade shortly. So irrespective of this working group I also go there on private business. I have quite a number of relatives and friends living there. And anyway, I still feel at home there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you still keep in touch with your acquaintances and colleagues of Albanian ethnicity living down there?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I have quite frequent encounters with them. When they come to Belgrade I see them there, not to mention telephone communications that we have. Friends are friends, and this lasts. Friendships last.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is your motive to devote your time to the destiny of the killed and missing persons?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that in the first place that this is a very important, serious, and responsible job. It is a question -- a humanitarian issue, because this is one of the most difficult issues which merits far greater intention than -- than it has today throughout the former Yugoslavia, and I hope that through my efforts I will contribute to discovering what happened to some of those missing people. Many of them are my friends and acquaintances. I am in touch with their relatives. Many reported that their relatives had gone missing, when they went missing, and when I was head of the district.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Odalovic, what is your principal occupation today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Due to circumstances I am unemployed. I am registered in the office of the unemployed, but as I said, I'm heading a commission which has a lot of work to do. But that's a different story, and I assume that doesn't interest you. If you're interested, I can explain. I was a deputy. My term expired. Then for six months we received our income according to our laws, and at the end of that period I didn't find employment anywhere; and I hope I will soon, but that is -- those are the facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is a district that you were a head of?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: A district is an administrative institution, a body formed by the government of the Republic of Serbia, and all its activities, all its responsibilities were carried out through the districts at the level of the whole Republic of Serbia. These are administrative activities, inspection, the things that have to be done on the ground and when citizens have the closest contacts with the state. Various demands, requests, complaints that they have. If you need more details, I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does a district have any jurisdiction with respect to security?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is the Kosovo district differ in any way from all the other districts on the territory of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: As far as districts are concerned, all of them have a uniform organisation throughout Serbia. In Kosovo and Metohija there were five, and in the whole of Serbia there were 29. We had the same responsibilities, the same tasks. We didn't all have the same territory nor the number of municipalities, but we couldn't go beyond our terms of reference which were identical for all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How many municipalities did the Kosovo district consist of?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: The Kosovo district consisted of 10 municipalities and was one of the largest in the Republic of Serbia in terms of territory, the number of inhabitants, and the number of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And to whom was the district responsible.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: Exclusively to the government of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Will you make a short break between my questions and your answers as we're speaking the same language. What was the relationship between the district and the Provisional Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: The districts were formed in 1992, and the Provisional Executive Council at the end of September 1998. The Provisional Executive Council and the district did not coincide in terms of responsibilities, because the laws of the Republic of Serbia were implemented by the district, whereas the Provisional Executive Council was an attempt -- or, rather, the intention by forming it was to set up provincial institutions and bodies, because this was needed on the ground, and those of us who were directly involved in affairs of government felt that such bodies needed to be set up in the province of Kosovo and Metohija so that the Albanians would vote in the election, that they would take over part of the executive powers; and the Provisional Executive Council was formed with that aim in mind. And it is important to note that this was the body that simply did not take over any of the responsibilities of the Kosovo district. It was a separate body, and I have described what its purpose was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And how long was it intended to last for?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: Its name indicates that it was of a temporary nature, until it achieves its mission. That is, until it ensures conditions for all the people in Kosovo and Metohija to cast their votes and take over their responsibilities. When Mr. Andjelkovic came and when we were discussing this, we felt that all these activities could be completed within a period of some nine months, and he asked for our full support. That is, we as heads of districts and having authority over local self-government should assist in the formation of those bodies and institutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, can you find a suitable place to interrupt again.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can break now. I forgot entirely about the break. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Odalovic, we have to break at this stage for half an hour and then resume at 7.00 -- at 6.00, sorry. Meanwhile, could you go with the usher from the courtroom, and we'll see you again at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Good afternoon again. I will repeat the question that I asked before we left for the break. Between the district and the temporary Executive Council or was there any overlap between those two bodies or was dealt with in a different way?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: There were no overlaps of jurisdiction between the two bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But there was some form of cooperation, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: Of course there was. Cooperation, the simple reason being the district happened to be in Kosovo and Metohija, the territory that the temporary Executive Council arrived in with a particular mandate, the mandate being to allow for normal life through the work of institutions, and this had to do with the municipalities -- rather, those units of self-government that existed in the district. Cooperation was necessary. More often than not, cooperation was intense, especially when talks began about a document that was supposed to regulate life in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about the jurisdiction of the district? Was it changed in 1999 or 1998?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: No. The jurisdiction of the district was not changed. It still had the same powers and the same job. However, events in 1998 and 1999, and above all, I mean the stepping up of terrorist activity and the many problems that arose as a result of that in the Kosovo district and throughout Kosovo and Metohija, certainly required even more intense involvement on our part, and efforts were being made to stabilise and normalise the situation. On the other hand, there was an increasing influx of foreign diplomats and journalists who, late in 1997 and throughout 1998, and this is something that I mentioned in a report, came in their hundreds to Kosovo and Metohija. There were all sorts of missions being set up. Therefore, as a district or, rather, as a group of districts we had to deal with that. That was part of our job. But, and I must repeat this, nobody took over any of our jurisdictions, any of our work, nor was this jurisdiction at any point reduced or amplified.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And then you had to organise everything during the state of war. So what I want to know is how did the civilian protection work?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: When the NATO aggression began and when a state of war was declared, the civilian protection was organised in keeping with the laws providing for this possibility. First there was the federal level and then this trickled down all the way to the district level or the municipal staffs of civilian protection. What was new in relation to the previous period, because the districts were a relatively new institution, there was the law on defence that was in force at the time, the law on defence of the Republic of Serbia, and this provided for a coordinating role of the civilian protection staffs. Each in their own areas. As a result, I specifically was appointed, by a decision of Mr. Geza Farkas, coordinator of the district civilian protection staff and the same thing happened in the remaining or, rather, throughout the Republic of Serbia, civilian protection staffs were organised under the same law and in keeping with the same legal provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the tasks were of the civilian protection since you were its commander in Kosovo and Metohija specifically during the war?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: Just for the sake of precision, let me repeat that I was the commander of the district civilian protection staff. As for our powers, these powers were based on law and included those civilian and military activities that in a state of peace would be left to the civilian protection; protecting citizens, putting them up. Whenever destruction occurred we had to deal with the consequences and repair any damage. Another thing that was typical, we had to gather livestock that was at large. We had to collect supplies that were past their sell-by date that could have left the population at risk. We had to take care of the water supplies and these were all civilian tasks. The civilian protection was an unarmed unit and units of the civilian protection bore no arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What were the relations to the MUP or possibly the army?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly we needed talks. We needed to exchange information. These were jobs, quite simply, that couldn't be done without joint assessments. However, the cooperation and the relations were more about exchanging information, about seeking assistance, about certain types of information. I think that is only natural and logical. Civilian Protection Units could not on their own know whether something was safe or whether where the bombs were falling and fragmentation projectiles, whether these areas were safe whether there were any terrorist units nearby. This form of cooperation was necessary because we could not complete our mandate without this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who was the Kosovo district civilian protection subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: I'll repeat about the law on defence. We were subordinated formally speaking to the republican protection staff which means that we were subordinated to federal bodies. That's how it is in terms of hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please don't explain. Just answer my questions. Let's move on to a different subject now. You were born and you lived for a long time in Kosovo and Metohija, didn't you? Are you familiar with the facts regarding the more recent history of the area? For example, its history in the Second World War, or should I perhaps ask you more specific question. Do you know what went on in the Drenica area towards the end of the Second World War and in its aftermath?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: I know a great deal about this. I wasn't alive at the time, needless to say, but my family, the place where I was born and many of the events that occurred, and I think history tells us a lot about these events and it would seem to indicate that in the period above all between 1941 and 1943, for the first time under Italy in Kosovo and Metohija, a state was created, an Albanian state. This caused a lot of destruction, a lot of expulsion of the population that lived in my area. My family or, more specifically, my mother's family was one of the families expelled at the time from their village. It was my native village and the greatest number of casualties were caused by the Albanian Balists.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We have to explain who the Balists were. You are using a term that you never explained, sir.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: The Balists were a quisling organisation. They worked with the fascists. They joined the fascist side, and they took up the political and strategic objective of setting up their own state. This led to a showdown with the Serbian population, the Montenegrin population and all the other ethnic groups, non-Albanian ethnic groups, they actively participated in the resistance struggle against the liberation army and they were the loyal servants of the fascist state of Italy.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If the question is continuing down this road of analysing the history, I would object to it as not being relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It appears to be very relevant to the statement made about doing what they did to them in Drenica, which is what it's all about. It's not about the history of Kosovo but it's about the particular event.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About General Naumann, if I may remind my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was the name of that organisation, sir, the Balists?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: One of the names that took hold in a way was Balicombatare [phoen]. I still owe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Balicombatare when Kosovo and Metohija was liberated from the Germans, what did the members of this group Balicombatare do?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: After the fall of fascist Germany and the breakdown of the Third Reich, a large scale rebellion erupted. The Balists were quite well organised and they continued to put up resistance, to the People's Liberation Army above all at the time, in a bid to keep the Drenica area, create an area in which they would be free to pursue their actions. Drenica is at the border itself. It is one of the border villages. My family comes from there. And the Balists burnt the village down, a total of 50 houses razed to the ground, which just shows that their intention was to expel everyone from the area, to cleanse the area and to create a state or an area that they could then rule with no hindrance, without the Serbs and without the Albanians [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Someone who is familiar with history, when they talk about the suppression of the Drenica rebellion in 1945 and 1946, what do they imply? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: The Drenica rebellion was put down. The People's Liberation Army started settling accounts with the Balist units. Coincidentally, I know this from the history of my family, over 4.000 members of the People's Liberation Army and those who were involved in crushing the Balist groups in the area were killed. Quite simply, this was Tito's army. That's what we called it, which comprised Albanians among other ethnic groups, and they were given task of settling accounts with these gangs to neutralise them and free Kosovo and Metohija just like the whole of Europe was liberated at the time. To all practical intents this was the last fascist stronghold after the breakdown of the Third Reich.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were civilians killed while the rebellion was being put down?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: Historians, politicians, and all those who know something about what went on, all those who followed what went on at the time and analysed what happened in Drenica never mention this. I can't rule out the fact that there were individual casualties amongst civilians at the time, but the gist was an armed rebellion was put down that had been organised by Balist gangs under the command of Saban Poloze [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just briefly, please. You're a native of the area. What do you think lies at the very foundation of all these clashes that occurred in the aftermath of the liberation in 1945, for example? In Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was the intention of the separatists to create another Albanian state in the area. This intention, this desire, has a history. I was alive in 1968 and I saw what happened. I was part of the rallies in Pristina. I was also alive back in 1971. I was an eyewitness to what went on. Rallies started on the 11th of March and continued throughout April. It was the students this time around who set up the same movement with the same demands. This continued in 1989 and 1990, all under the same aegis with the same objectives. The intention being to create a state within Kosovo and Metohija. Unfortunately, we see the same thing happening all over again today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Whereas a discourse into the history might have been to some degree relevant, the objection now is that this evidence being elicited is not referred to or properly referred to in the 65 ter summary that is filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you say that, are you referring to the evidence about Drenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The evidence about Drenica, but in particular the evidence about the events of the '70s, 1969.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. But also saying that Drenica wasn't referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, why is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have just made a brief overview. This was just one single question about the history of Kosovo. I have no intention of dealing with that any longer. This was just this one question, and the witness is living there and he knows what's going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're ignoring my question about Drenica. Why was that not referred to in your 65 ter?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I probably forgot. I didn't think it was all that important, because it is one of the events of the history of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's a limited extent to which your birth certificate is going to be a shield for you, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must be that. There's no other explanation. I thought that was a global overview of Kosovo that the witness was giving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not that the real complaint is about because the Prosecution have a number of witness who is have given evidence of a fairly general nature about the various events in 1971 and 1989 and 1990, but something as specific as Drenica is clearly a matter that should have been heralded in a 65 ter summary. Anyway, the damage has been done and we must proceed so, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour. It's my mistake then. Let us now move on to 1997, as I have no intention to talk about history any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you please explain the situation in Kosovo and Metohija as of 1997? How would you describe it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: What is characteristic of 1997 is that that was the first time in public, as far as I can remember, at a funeral in Metohija armed and trained groups of people appeared in uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please stop for a moment. Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- and I'm not one to object to everything, but 1997, if we're on that track that is not something referred to in this summary, 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think on this occasion, Mr. Fila, you should -- you should confine yourself now to what you have given notice of. You've benefited obviously already in failing to --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm talking about the development of events. I can ask the questions about 1998 and again we'll come to 1997. It is just the evolution of the events and of the situation in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You deal with what's in your 65 ter summary and then we'll see whether something else coincidentally emerges.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please explain the situation in 1998, the year covered by the indictment. What happens? What happened then?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: What is characteristic of 1998 is that the terrorist activities by terrorist groups became more and more intensified. They -- there were more and more attacks on civilians in 1998, on policemen, more and more kidnappings, blockades of roads. Simply we have an increasingly well-organised action by these bands, and their aim was, as they unfortunately managed to achieve briefly in 1998, to separate a part of the area of Metohija which includes Drenica, unfortunately, and to gain full control of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there any specific incident which was particularly disturbing in the spring of 1998 onwards?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: In the first half of 1998 there were several serious incidents. One of them was certainly the event in the village of Prekaz when one of those groups and gangs was neutralised. Unfortunately, in this conflict in which security organs participate, who first tried to arrest Adem Jashari, civilians were also killed. I think it was in January, February 1998. Then some other very important events which disturbed the entire population of Kosovo and Metohija were attacks on Orahovac, kidnappings.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did the events in neighbouring Albania have any impact, and the appearance of the KLA? Did this affect the situation in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely what I was saying. The intensification of these terrorist activities in 1997 and 1998 were most directly linked to developments in Albania because it was then when an enormous quantity of ammunition and weapons were transferred to the territory of Kosovo and Metohija and especially in Metohija, and that means Drenica. Some people were armed of their own free will, others at first by force. In any event, hundreds of thousands of long barrels crossed illegally the state frontier and entered Kosovo and Metohija and were distributed to the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that they took control of a part of Kosovo, and what about the other parts of Kosovo that were not taken control of by this group? Wasn't life normal there? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: In the most part of Kosovo and Metohija life was normal. What was happening in Metohija fortunately did not spread to the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija, which doesn't mean to say there weren't isolated incidents, but in any event, there were no blockades of roads or interruptions of communications, nor were there large groups or bands that were attacking large settlements as was the case with Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the strength of the KLA and the influence of Rugova?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rugova, in the '90s, that is at the end of the '80s and the beginning of '90s was an absolute leader among the Albanians. At elections that they themselves organised in 1992, he was elected president. His relationship to the so-called liberation army was not a relationship that could be described as one of cooperation or sympathy. In fact, my impression was that these were two opposing options heading towards the same goal. Mr. Rugova never gave up the idea of creating a state, but at least to the best of my knowledge; and I had contacts with some people who were close to him, he did not wish to achieve that by force of arms as opposed to the leaders of the KLA who sought to achieve that goal by force of arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know that representatives of the government of the Republic of Serbia came to negotiate with the politicians of large Albanian parties such as Mr. Rugova and others in this period of 1998?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that. There were several such attempts in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We've heard a number of witnesses, so let us not waste any more time. Do you know how invitations were handed to Albanian politicians to attend these meetings?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: I do know for the simple reason that most of these invitations were handed via the office of the Kosovo district, that -- through my service, so a courier from my office would carry these invitations to the leaders of the Albanian political parties and hand in these invitations and -- to them at their addresses. I apologise. Just one further comment. As for Mr. Rugova, his office was in the Writers' Association of Kosovo, in the very centre of Pristina, and that is where Mr. Adnan Merovci signed that he received the invitation. So his signature is a guarantee that those invitation were received.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did the other Albanian politicians behave in the summer of 1998 in relation to the KLA, and how did they behave later on?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: Up until the summer of 1998, public sympathy towards the so-called KLA was shown only by Adem Demaci. All the other leaders on the political stage among the Albanians were quite reserved. However, one event, at least that is my own judgement, overturned the entire situation, and that was when Mr. Holbrooke, at the end of June, mid-June, I can't remember the exact date, did something in UNMIK which in general opinion was the most direct support of these terrorist bands, and after that among the political leaders of other Albanian parties, their behaviour started to change; and they started to extend greater support to this so-called liberation army.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: For the transcript, there's an error in the interpretation. It says UNMIK and it should be Junik place, a settlement in Kosovo and Metohija between Decani and Djakovica. Could you please, but very quickly because we've heard quite a number of witnesses about the same issue, tell us what was the situation in Kosovo and Metohija in the spring and summer of 1998. Give us a very quick overview.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: Extremely difficult. Almost a third of the territory was under the control of these armed bands. More than 80 villages which until then were inhabited by Serbs, Montenegrins, and other non-Albanians were ethnically cleansed. I think we had more than 4.500 displaced persons in 1998. There were very serious incidents of mass kidnappings, miners at the mines in Bilacevac, in Retimlje, and Opterusa where more than 60 civilians were taken from their homes. The attack on Orahovac. All this among the Serbs and other non-Albanians caused a great deal of concern, and fear, and there was obvious panic. So people started to move out their families to central Serbia. Some of them came to the part of the territory which was not the site of serious conflicts, but Metohija, Drenica, and some villages around Podujevo had been ethnically cleansed and were under the control of terrorist bands. And what was particularly alarming was that at the end of June or the beginning of July, they almost reached Pristina. They took control of the coal mines at Bilacevac which was of major significance as a source of energy, and this most seriously disturbed people in Kosovo Polje, Obilic, and Pristina, because somehow the limit had been crossed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were there problems with the communications?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: Most of the vital communications in the area of Metohija were interrupted. Whoever would take those roads was at risk. One of the strategic routes, Pec-Pristina, were inaccessible. The roads towards Glogovac, from Mitrovica towards Srbica as well, so that communication was extremely difficult and unsafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Have you been given the documents, please? I'd like you to have a look at them. Could you take a look at tab 1, please. Defence Exhibit 2D364. What document are we talking about? What is it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document containing a list of citizens and members of the MUP who in the period from 1st January to 1st of July, 1998, were abducted by Albanian terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do we have on the list only names of Serbs or are there others as well?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: On this list, in addition to names of Serbs and Montenegrins, there are names of citizens of Albanian, Romany, and other ethnicities which the terrorists had hijacked -- I'm sorry, kidnapped, and also six members of the police who suffered the same fate. They, too, were kidnapped by Albanian terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did they ever return?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that I head the commission for missing persons, by briefing looking at these names I can say with certainty that more than 90 per cent of these persons have not -- have not returned to their families to this day. Their destiny is unknown. And as for members of the police as we matched with the MUP of the Republic of Serbia the names of those missing, I can tell you that out of these six, five are still missing. And the same applies to the miners kidnapped at Bilacevac on the 22nd of June. Nothing is none about their fate either. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why were these Albanians kidnapped?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: As for the kidnapping of Albanians, this was precisely the objective and the intention of the terrorists, in order to crush any resistance or stop anybody from thinking differently, the aim being to intimidate all those -- well, I see here now that some of these Albanians who were kidnapped were actually employed. They worked in companies and institutions, and the aim of the terrorists was for Albanians to leave those companies, institutions. They made promises to them that once they were in power they would bring them all back. And this made it easier for them when undertaking certain activities they knew that there were no Albanians among those people. And if you look at this, they are workers of the Stimlje Plantation. Included here this is the part of the Kosovo district. So these are workers who were employees of Srbija Sume in Trepca. So in essence, this was the objective and this was the intention behind what the terrorists did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Could you look at tab 2 now, please, 2D372. That is the exhibit number. What is that? Comment briefly, please, because we've heard other witnesses on this document.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: But I have to read it first, don't I. This is a dramatic appeal, I would say, by Andjelko Kolasinac who was a representative of the Orahovac Municipal Assembly. He talks about the critical situation that prevailed in the area at the time. He is requesting assistance from official bodies. You see that it was forwarded to the government, to the MUP in Orahovac and Prizren and to the command of an area in Prizren. He was seeking assistance. He was asking for help. He knew obviously that what was going on on the ground at the time was very serious and based on what I can see here, he's trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Odalovic, was this sent to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In that case, we don't need Mr. Odalovic to tell us what the letter says, which is what he's actually continuing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fair enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now my other question, so don't comment. What was the situation in your district in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that in relation to what the situation was in Metohija ours was much better. In my area there were certain problems. In Glogovac municipality, in Podujevo municipality, in Stimlje and parts of Kacanik, while the other areas were relatively peaceful with sporadic incidents occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about all these events that you've described and the general situation? Was there any reaction by the Serbian state? Was there any reaction by Yugoslavia, and what was the reaction, if so, in the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: All of us were sending such appeals to the state bodies. We asked the state, we appealed to the state to protect the people, the buildings, all the facilities, the companies, because at this point in time the operations conducted by these terrorist gangs were putting everything at risk; and I think this is something that is a well-known fact. There were certain anti-terrorist activities that followed as a result of these appeals. So throughout this period there erupted a serious -- a serious -- clashes with these gangs. For the first time, and that is what is particularly noteworthy about this, the state decided to settle accounts once and for all with these terrorist gangs simply because the state territory was under threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did these developments effect the humanitarian situation in Kosovo and Metohija, and what did the state do about that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: All of this caused large-scale humanitarian problems in terms of supplies, above all but also in terms of how free people were to move about or leave their homes. This called for an intervention on the part of the state bodies. The state stepped in in June. The federal and republican government set up a staff to provide supplies to people in an organised manner. I was a member of the central headquarters of Kosovo and Metohija and we also set up local offices elsewhere to bring supplies to the local population, the objective being to bring supplies and to help people who were in a very difficult situation at the time, to help them in both humanitarian terms and also to make possible that people had all the supplies the necessary supplies throughout Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Odalovic we have heard a witness who talked at great length about it can you tell us briefly about what sort of aid we're looking at how this aid was distributed and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: There were displaced people and there were those in need and they all required humanitarian aid. We worked with the Red Cross. We worked with bodies of local self-government and our own people helped to set up humanitarian -- humanitarian aid distribution centres in certain localities. We did this in keeping with the norms based on the monthly need of any citizen. A litre of oil, eight kilogrammes of flour, sugar and so on and so forth. These are details I'm not going into that. We made sure there was enough energy of any kind for life to go on normally. This was something that was an enormous problem another aspect was state intervention in terms of sufficient quantities being secured in as far as possible from the state's commodity reserves. There was a lot of shady business at the time. People started smuggling these goods. The goods were overpriced. The tariffs were far to high for the population and some people were making enormous profits. The objective on our part was to put this under control. The third aspect, which also tells you something about what we did was this: according to these norms, each and every citizen of Kosovo and Metohija needed an opportunity through socially owned companies and shops on the ground to purchase these goods at regulated prices and each and every citizen of Kosovo and Metohija needed access to these things regardless of any of their differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was any aid offered in terms of repairing houses, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: Just before this, and I can't remember the exact date, the directorate for regional development was set up in Kosovo and Metohija. This directorate was established by the government of the Republic of Serbia. It was through Serbia's development fund that certain amounts of building material and everything else that was required for repairs was brought there. There was a lot of destruction and there were consequences. The directorate was quite successful in general. There were areas that were never reached by this aid because terrorist activity continued in those areas. On the other hand, they did everything within their power for Albanians who were offered this sort of aid to refuse to have it. They were trying to create a different media image, to show the destruction and the destruction in all of its consequences and they wanted to make this come across as if nobody really wanted repairs. The directorate, and I remember this one meeting we had, invested over 2 million in funds in repairs and reconstruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What figure did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: 200 million dinars it's very hard to convert now but that was the reported figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the implementation of the education agreement in Kosovo and Metohija in 1998? And perhaps -- well, could you go to tab 3, please. Defence Exhibit 2D2. Tab 4. Defence Exhibit 2D3. Please comment briefly.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: These two documents are in relation to an agreement that was previously signed, the education agreement. Actually, with the assistance of Sant'Egidio, an Italian organisation, and Monsignor Paglia an agreement was reached that both Mr. Milosevic and Rugova signed on the normalisation of issues regarding education. This was one of the most burning issues in Kosovo and Metohija. What this shows is that with the assistance of some other organisations as well and first and foremost I'm here referring to issues to do with reconstruction. I don't know who else was involved. They started implementing this agreement. This is how the agreement looked in purely operational terms. Certain buildings were to be built, certain buildings were to be repaired. And the other document also talks about the fact that the intention was to build a number of new buildings and facilities. The students and pupils were to be given more room. This was primarily about secondary school students because Albanians students had remained outside the university up until that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were any of your people involved in this?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: Whenever the government and the state bodies took up a certain responsibility, all of us who were part of the system would receive instructions and would have the responsibility of being involved. In addition to Mr. Milivoje Simonovic who was the focal point for this project I see Mr. Milan Canovic who was the head of a department in my district. The ministry of construction. We were a whole unit. There were eight of us and we were all involved in implementing these tasks. We believed this to be a priority, our objective being to make sure that the 3 plus 3 Agreement would be implemented by the academic year on the 1st of September what this meant is the Albanian students who up to that point had remained outside the work of the university would now be back to continue their education in the all the public institutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you remind me what the 3 plus 3 Agreement was?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness. Can you remind me what the 3 plus 3 Agreement was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 3 plus 3 Agreement was signed by Mr. Rugova and Mr. Milosevic in September 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You need say no more. I'm simply confused by the use of more than one name for it. Please continue, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Briefly. Let's move through this as quickly as possible. What about the -- giving more room to university students and was there resistance from any quarters as far as this intention was concerned?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: This was implemented. I don't have the details of that later agreement, but as far as I remember the government of the Republic of Serbia had its own group comprising Percevic, Bjeletic, and some other persons, as well as Mr. Ganja [phoen] who took part in the implementation of this project on behalf of Mr. Rugova, if I remember correctly; and I might go wrong on this, there were about 42 square metres of room and most of it was devoted to teaching in the Albanian language. 42.000 square metres. That was reaction among those teaching the Serbian language and the students. There was fear quite simply that their interests were at stake, their positions would be jeopardised. There was fear of new incidents occurring. There was a certain amount of resistance but the state determined that this was a priority task. So despite all the resistance those most directly involved despite all managed to see this through and give more room as had been agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you go to tab 5 now, sir. 2D373. I only have two minutes left, sir. If you could please use those two minutes well and answer my question. What's this about?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, there is no Serbian translation but I believe I can understand this document. I am quite familiar with the subject matter after all. This is the memorandum of the so-called Republic of Kosovo which didn't exist at the time and secretariat or, rather, the ministry, education ministry. The fund is being requested here to secure that there was sufficient chairs and desks for a total of 13 schools in the Pristina area. In Pristina municipality these are preparations obviously not quite preparations because the academic year has already started but obviously the people from elementary schools has run out of chairs and desks throughout Kosovo and Metohija; and what I can say based on this document is that these are state institutions, buildings, schools that belonged to the state of Serbia or to its local units and teaching in the Albanian language went on with no interruptions with no hindrance. We made sure they had electricity, firewood at one point in time we paid help people who were assisting the schools. At no point in time was this a problem. If they addressed us for these desks and chairs I'm sure we would have somehow made funds available to somehow secure the equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was the reason you accepted something like this?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO ODALOVIC
utterances.text: Our objective was to stop anyone who was trying to manipulate children. We didn't want children not going to school although the conditions were irregular. We gave them buildings and schools so that children wouldn't go to private homes and attend facilities that just weren't appropriate. We simply opened the doors of all schools to everyone, elementary schools, and in part also secondary schools and we made it possible for them to be taught in their native language in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, lest you should warn me, I think this is a got time to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I clarify with you, Mr. Odalovic, the English version of this document relates to the supply, by the Republic of Kosovo Municipal Education Board, of furniture. Now, these -- the indication is that this was furniture that was not supplied by the Republic of Serbia. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that. In case you understood me to be saying that. I said if they had addressed us we -- we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand your evidence that if they would have asked you, you would have of found the funds for it, but it's the nature of the document I want to be clear about. The nature of the document is coming from -- it's a communication from the Republic of Kosovo which you say was not properly constituted and should not be recognised, and it relates to the provision of furniture through a foundation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. The Republic of Kosovo never existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which means that this is a ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the desks existed. That's another matter. But thank you for helping us. Mr. Odalovic, we have to bring the proceedings to an end for this week at this stage and we will resume at 9.00 on Monday.
